scenes.heading: Isomers
scenes.say: Isomers have the same molecular formula but a different arrangement of atoms. That can change the boiling point, the smell, and even how a medicine acts in your body.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: LISTEN and SILENT: same letters, different words
scenes.science: Isomers: same molecular formula, different compounds
scenes.breaks: you can rearrange letters any way, but atoms must follow bonding rules, like carbon always making four bonds.
scenes.say: The letters in listen also spell silent: same letters, different words. Isomers are the same. Ethanol and methoxymethane are both C two H six O, but one is an alcohol that boils at about seventy-eight degrees, and the other is a gas at room temperature.
scenes.caption: The letters in LISTEN also spell SILENT: same letters, different words. Isomers are the same. Ethanol and methoxymethane are both C₂H₆O, but one is an alcohol that boils at about 78 °C, and the other is a gas at room temperature.

scenes.heading: Structural isomers
points: Positional: group in a different place
scenes.say: Structural isomers have atoms joined in a different order. Remember chain, place, group. Change the branching, like butane and methylpropane. Move the group, like propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol. Or swap the group, like propanal and propanone.

scenes.heading: Cis vs trans

left.title: cis-but-2-ene
points: Both CH₃ on the same side

scenes.say: Cis and trans isomers exist because a C double bond C can't rotate. Cis means same side; trans means across. You need two different groups on each carbon of the double bond, so but-1-ene, with two hydrogens on carbon one, has none.
scenes.caption: Cis and trans isomers exist because a C=C can't rotate. Cis means same side; trans means across. You need two different groups on each carbon of the double bond, so but-1-ene, with two hydrogens on C1, has none.

scenes.heading: Chiral centres
points: Chiral centre: C with four different groups
Rule out CH₂, CH₃, C=C and C=O carbons
Racemic 50:50 mix: no rotation of light
scenes.say: A chiral centre is a carbon with four different groups. It gives two enantiomers, mirror images that can't be stacked, like left and right football boots. Quickly rule out any C H two, C H three, or double-bonded carbon.
scenes.caption: A chiral centre is a carbon with four different groups. It gives two enantiomers, mirror images that can't be stacked, like left and right football boots. Quickly rule out any CH₂, CH₃, or double-bonded carbon.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Does 2-chlorobutane, CH₃CHClCH₂CH₃, have a chiral centre or cis/trans isomers?
lines: No C=C, so no cis/trans isomers
scenes.say: Look at carbon two. It holds hydrogen, chlorine, a methyl and an ethyl group. All four are different, so it's a chiral centre, and there are two enantiomers. There's no double bond, so no cis or trans isomers.

scenes.heading: Why enantiomers matter
points: Can act differently in the body
scenes.say: Enantiomers have the same boiling point and density. But they rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions, and chiral receptors in your body can tell them apart. That's why the two forms of carvone smell different, and why thalidomide caused such harm.

points: Enantiomers differ in light and life
scenes.say: Quick recap. Structural isomers have different names: chain, place, group. Cis and trans need a locked double bond. A chiral carbon has four different groups, giving mirror-image enantiomers. Now try the practice questions!
